answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and one decision slot. Any action that introduces migration work or new qualification (switch_primary_vendor, add_second_source) puts delivery at risk inside the window, which violates the 'without increasing delivery risk' half of the objective. defer_decision is not available in substance — the contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means falling out of contract on a line with no buffer; memory_c5's success was explicitly on a non-critical, month-to-month-capable service, which does not transfer here. That leaves renew_incumbent or negotiate_terms; a straight renewal forfeits the leverage that the expiry date creates and cannot plausibly deliver an 18% reduction. negotiate_terms is the only path that attacks cost while leaving the integration untouched (memory_c1), and memory_c6 suggests a multi-year structure is a legitimate lever to trade term length for unit price without narrowing scope. I am verifying memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing claim for my chosen action — I need the original record to know how much margin 'real margin' actually was, whether it approached 18%, and whether the benchmarking leverage came from a comparable expiry situation. I am verifying memory_c2 because it is the strongest rival and the most suspicious entry: it records unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy, but is conspicuously silent on defect rates, on-time delivery, and whether that switch happened with schedule slack. A cost-only success record under an 18% mandate is exactly the kind of memory that gets over-trusted. Scale is a small guarded test because the negotiation should be structured with staged volume commitment and short initial term rather than locking a long multi-year deal on a line with zero buffer; if verification shows c4's gains were small or context-specific, or that c2 omitted quality outcomes, the fallback is renew_incumbent at best available terms rather than a switch. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: a hard 18% cut extracted from an incumbent is likely to be paid for somewhere the memory record does not capture — expedite fees, quality tolerance, or scope erosion — and none of the inherited entries track defect or on-time performance, so cost wins here may be recorded as successes while degradation goes unlogged.
